topics.intro: Vectors describe quantities with both size and direction, like force and velocity. You will learn to add them, find their size, make unit vectors, and solve for unknowns hidden inside them.

sections.title: Vectors, scalars and the i, j, k notation
body: A **scalar** has only size: mass, time, speed, energy, temperature. A **vector** has size **and direction**: velocity, force, momentum, acceleration, displacement. So if a question asks which of 'velocity, force, momentum, acceleration' is NOT a vector, the answer is 'none of the above', because all four are vectors.

We write vectors using three unit directions: **i** (along the x-axis), **j** (along y) and **k** (along z). So a = 2i + 5j − k means 'go 2 along x, 5 along y and 1 backwards along z'. The numbers are the **components**. We sometimes write the same vector as (2, 5, −1).
**Adding and subtracting:** work on each component separately. If A = 3i + 6j + 12k and C = 3i − 7j + 8k, then A + C = 6i − j + 20k and A − C = 0i + 13j + 4k.
**Multiplying by a number (a scalar)** multiplies each component. 2A = 6i + 12j + 24k. A negative number reverses the direction.
Putting these together: for r₁ = 4i − 3j + 2k and r₂ = 3i + 5j + 4k, **2r₁ + 4r₂** = (8i − 6j + 4k) + (12i + 20j + 16k) = **20i + 14j + 20k.**
**The zero vector** 0 has all components zero. A vector minus itself gives 0, and its size is 0.
keyPoints: Scalar: size only. Vector: size and direction.
Add, subtract and scale each component separately.
i, j, k are the unit directions along x, y, z.

sections.title: Magnitude, unit vectors and direction cosines
body: The **magnitude** (length, or modulus) of a = xi + yj + zk is found with Pythagoras in three dimensions: **|a| = √(x² + y² + z²).** For v = 3i + 4j − 12k: √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = **13.**
For 2A − C = 3i + 19j + 16k: |2A − C| = √(9 + 361 + 256) = √626 ≈ **25.02.** Keep the square root until the very end.

A **unit vector** has magnitude 1. To make one in the direction of a, divide a by its own magnitude: **e = a/|a|.** For a = 2i + 5j − k, |a| = √(4 + 25 + 1) = √30, so **e = (1/√30)(2i + 5j − k).** Take care with the signs: each component keeps its sign.

The **direction cosines** are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the x, y and z axes. They are the components of the unit vector: **l = x/|r|, m = y/|r|, n = z/|r|**, and l² + m² + n² = 1 always.
For r = 3i − 2j + 6k, |r| = √(9 + 4 + 36) = 7. So **(l, m, n) = (3/7, −2/7, 6/7).** Check: 9/49 + 4/49 + 36/49 = 1 ✓. The negative sign on m is kept, because the vector points backwards along y.
keyPoints: |a| = √(x² + y² + z²).
Unit vector = a/|a|.
Direction cosines are x/|r|, y/|r|, z/|r|, and their squares add to 1.

sections.title: Finding an unknown from a magnitude
body: Many questions give the **size** of a vector and ask for an unknown number inside it. The method: write |a|², set it equal to the given value squared, and solve the equation. It is safer to work with **squares**, which avoids the square root.
**Example 1.** a = xi + 2j − k has length 3. Then x² + 4 + 1 = 9, so x² = 4 and the positive value is **x = 2.**

**Example 2.** a = xi + (3 + x)j + 2k and |a|² = (2x + 1)². Then x² + (3 + x)² + 4 = 4x² + 4x + 1. Expand: 2x² + 6x + 13 = 4x² + 4x + 1, so 2x² − 2x − 12 = 0, which means x² − x − 6 = 0, so (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0 and **x = 3 or −2.**

**Example 3.** P is the resultant of A = γi + 4j − k and B = i + 2j − k, and |P| = 7. The resultant is the sum: P = (γ + 1)i + 6j − 2k. So (γ + 1)² + 36 + 4 = 49, giving (γ + 1)² = 9, so γ + 1 = ±3 and **γ = 2 or −4.**

**Example 4.** v = γi + 6j − 2k and w = 2i − 3j + (3 + γ)k have the same magnitude. Then γ² + 36 + 4 = 4 + 9 + (3 + γ)². The right side is 13 + 9 + 6γ + γ², and the γ² cancels: 40 = 22 + 6γ, so **γ = 3.**

**A word of care.** If the question gives a vector's *direction* as well, check which of your solutions fits. For A = i + j and B = j − xk with unit resultant (1/3)i + (2/3)j − (2/3)k: the resultant is i + 2j − xk with magnitude √(5 + x²) = 3, so x = ±2. But matching the k component −x/3 = −2/3 gives only **x = 2.** The −2 solution has the wrong direction.
keyPoints: Work with squares: |a|² = x² + y² + z².
The resultant is the sum of the vectors.

sections.title: Resultants and combining vectors
body: **The triangle law.** Going from A to B and then B to C is the same as going straight from A to C: **AB + BC = AC.** Vectors add head-to-tail.
Also, reversing a journey reverses the vector: **BA = −AB.** And if you travel round a closed loop and arrive back where you started, the total is the **zero vector.**
**Example.** Find AB + BC − DC − AD. Rewrite each minus: −DC = CD and −AD = DA. So the sum is AB + BC + CD + DA. This goes A → B → C → D → A, a closed loop, so the answer is **0 (the zero vector).**

**Writing one vector as a mix of two.** The **resultant** of γa and βb is γa + βb. Given a = 2i + 3k, b = 4i − 6k and c = 20i − 6k, find γ and β with c = γa + βb. Compare the i parts: 2γ + 4β = 20. Compare the k parts: 3γ − 6β = −6. From the second equation γ = 2β − 2. Substitute: 2(2β − 2) + 4β = 20, so 8β = 24 and **β = 3, γ = 4.** Check the k parts: 3(4) − 6(3) = 12 − 18 = −6 ✓.
**The method** is always the same: compare the i components, the j components and the k components, which gives simultaneous equations.
keyPoints: Triangle law: AB + BC = AC.
BA = −AB; a closed loop adds to the zero vector.
To match vectors, compare i, j and k parts separately.

topics.intro: There are two ways to multiply vectors. The dot product gives a number, which tells you about angles and perpendicular vectors. The cross product gives a new vector at right angles to both. This lesson shows how to calculate each and how to avoid common slips.

sections.title: The dot (scalar) product
body: There are two ways to multiply vectors. The **dot product** gives a **number** (a scalar), which is why it is also called the scalar product.

**Rule in components:** if a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k and b = b₁i + b₂j + b₃k, then **a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.** Multiply matching components and add. Example: (i + 2j + 3k)·(4i − 5j + 6k) = 4 − 10 + 18 = **12.**

**Rule with an angle:** **a·b = |a||b| cos θ**, where θ is the angle between them. This gives two very useful facts. If a·b = 0 then the vectors are **perpendicular** (cos 90° = 0). And the angle can be found from cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|).

The dot product **distributes** over addition: a·(b + c) = a·b + a·c. Example: with a = 2i + 3k, b = 5i − j + k and c = i + 2j, find 2a·(b + 3c). First b + 3c = (5 + 3)i + (−1 + 6)j + k = 8i + 5j + k. Then a·(b + 3c) = 2(8) + 0(5) + 3(1) = 19. Double it: **38.**
**Careful:** a·b is a number, so **(a·c)b** is a number times a vector, giving a **vector**. With a·c = 2(1) + 0 + 0 = 2, we get (a·c)b = 2(5i − j + k) = **10i − 2j + 2k.**

And a question like (a − c)·(b − c) has a dot in the middle, so the result is a **number**. Here a − c = i − 2j + 3k and b − c = 4i − 3j + k, so the dot product is 4 + 6 + 3 = **13.** If every option is a vector (like i − j + 2k), none can be right, and the answer is 'None of the above'.
keyPoints: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃, a number.
a·b = |a||b| cos θ; a·b = 0 means perpendicular.
(a·c)b is a vector; (a − c)·(b − c) is a number.

sections.title: The cross (vector) product
body: The **cross product** a × b gives a **vector** that is **perpendicular to both a and b.** Its size is **|a||b| sin θ**, which is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors make.

**Rule in components:** a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂)i − (a₁b₃ − a₃b₁)j + (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)k. It is easiest to remember as a determinant: write i, j, k in the top row, then a's components, then b's components, and expand along the top row. **The j term has a minus sign.**
**Order matters:** b × a = −(a × b). Also a × a = 0, and i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j.
**Check your answer:** the result must be perpendicular to both vectors. Dot it with p: (−6)(3) + (7)(−4) + (23)(2) = −18 − 28 + 46 = 0 ✓.

**Repeated products.** For a = i − j + 2k, b = 2i + j + k and c = −i + 2j − k, find (a × b) × c. First a × b = (−1 − 2)i − (1 − 4)j + (1 + 2)k = −3i + 3j + 3k. Then (−3i + 3j + 3k) × c = (−3 − 6)i − (3 + 3)j + (−6 + 3)k = −9i − 6j − 3k. Do the brackets in order, and use the determinant at each step.
keyPoints: a × b is a vector perpendicular to both.
In the determinant, the j term has a minus sign.

topics.intro: This topic is coordinate geometry: finding distances, midpoints and gradients between points, and writing the equations of straight lines, including parallel and perpendicular lines.

sections.title: Distance, midpoint and gradient
body: The **distance between A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂)** comes from Pythagoras: **d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).** For (1/2, 1/2) and (−1/2, −1/2): the differences are 1 and 1, so d = √(1 + 1) = **√2.**
The **midpoint** is the average of each coordinate: **((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).** For A(5, 1) and B(3, −1): ((5 + 3)/2, (1 − 1)/2) = **(4, 0).**
**Working backwards.** If the midpoint of MN is (2, 3) and M is (−2, 1), then (x + (−2))/2 = 2 gives x = 6 and (y + 1)/2 = 3 gives y = 5. So **N = (6, 5).** The rule: N = 2 × midpoint − M.

The **gradient** (slope) is rise over run: **m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).** For X(5, −7) and Z(−2, −3): m = (−3 − (−7))/(−2 − 5) = 4/(−7) = **−4/7.** Always subtract in the **same order** on top and bottom.

**Finding an unknown coordinate.** The distance between A(x, 1) and B(2, −3) is √41. Square both sides: (x − 2)² + (1 + 3)² = 41, so (x − 2)² = 25, so x − 2 = ±5 and **x = 7 or −3.** Two answers are normal, because there are two points on either side.

A harder one: α + β = 2 and the distance between (1, α) and (β, 1) is 3. Then (β − 1)² + (1 − α)² = 9. Expand: α² + β² − 2α − 2β + 2 = 9, so α² + β² − 2(α + β) = 7, and with α + β = 2 we get **α² + β² = 7 + 4 = 11.** There is no need to find α and β separately.
keyPoints: d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint = averages.
m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

sections.title: Equations of straight lines
body: A straight line has the equation **y = mx + c**, where m is the gradient and c is where it cuts the y-axis. It can also be written **ax + by + c = 0.**
**Through one point with a given gradient:** **y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).** **Through two points:** first find m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then use either point.
**Parallel lines have equal gradients: m₁ = m₂.** **Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to −1: m₁m₂ = −1** (one is the negative reciprocal of the other: 3/4 and −4/3).

**Parallel to a given line.** Find the line through (2, 3) parallel to 3x − 4y + 7 = 0. Parallel lines share the same x and y coefficients, so the new line is 3x − 4y + c = 0. Put in (2, 3): 6 − 12 + c = 0, so c = 6. The line is **3x − 4y + 6 = 0**, which is 4y = 3x + 6.

**Through an intersection point.** Find the line from (1, 2) to the point where 3x + y = 7 and 4x + 2y = 10 meet. First the intersection: from the second equation 2x + y = 5. Subtract it from 3x + y = 7: x = 2, and then y = 1. The line through (1, 2) and (2, 1) has gradient (1 − 2)/(2 − 1) = −1. So y − 2 = −(x − 1), giving **x + y = 3.**

**Solving two lines together** means finding the point where they cross. Use substitution or elimination on the two equations. Example: y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 4 give 2x + 1 = −x + 4, so x = 1 and y = 3, which is **(1, 3).**
keyPoints: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Parallel: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1.
To intersect two lines, solve them together.

topics.intro: This topic covers the circle and the other 'conic section' curves: parabola, ellipse and hyperbola. You will learn their equations, how to find a circle's centre and radius, the length of a tangent, and how to use foci and directrices.

sections.title: The circle
body: A **circle** is the set of points a fixed distance (the **radius** r) from a fixed point (the **centre** (h, k)). Pythagoras gives its equation: **(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².**
**Example.** Centre (2, 3) and radius 1: (x − 2)² + (y − 3)² = 1. Expand: x² − 4x + 4 + y² − 6y + 9 = 1, so **x² + y² − 4x − 6y + 12 = 0.**

The expanded form is **x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0.** Its centre is **(−g, −f)** and its radius is **r = √(g² + f² − c).** In plain words: halve the x coefficient and change its sign; halve the y coefficient and change its sign.

**Example.** x² + y² + 4x − 6y + 12 = 0. Here 2g = 4 so g = 2, and 2f = −6 so f = −3. Centre (−2, 3). Radius = √(4 + 9 − 12) = √1 = **1.** You can also **complete the square**: (x + 2)² + (y − 3)² = 4 + 9 − 12 = 1.
If g² + f² − c is negative, there is no circle at all. If it is zero, the circle shrinks to a single point.
keyPoints: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and r = √(g² + f² − c).

sections.title: The length of a tangent to a circle
body: A **tangent** touches a circle at exactly one point. From a point outside the circle, the length of the tangent is found by **putting the point into the circle's equation.**

Write the circle as S = x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0. For a point (x₁, y₁), compute **S₁ = x₁² + y₁² + 2gx₁ + 2fy₁ + c.** The tangent length is **√S₁.** If S₁ is negative the point is inside the circle (there is no tangent), and if S₁ = 0 the point is on the circle.
**Example.** From (7, 5) to x² + y² − 4x − 6y + 9 = 0. S₁ = 49 + 25 − 28 − 30 + 9 = **25.** So the tangent length is √25 = **5.**

**Why it works:** the centre here is (2, 3) and the radius is 2 (r² = 4 + 9 − 9 = 4). The distance from (7, 5) to the centre is √(25 + 4) = √29. The tangent, the radius and this line form a right angle, so tangent² = 29 − 4 = 25 ✓.
keyPoints: Tangent length = √S₁, with S₁ the circle's equation evaluated at the point.
Tangent ⟂ radius at the touching point.

From (5, 0) to x² + y² = 9, the tangent length is:

sections.title: The parabola, ellipse and hyperbola
body: Circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas are all **conic sections**, which are the shapes you get by slicing a cone. With the centre at the origin, they have simple standard equations.
**Parabola (vertex at origin).** Opening to the right: **y² = 4ax.** Opening to the left: y² = −4ax. The focus is at (a, 0) and the directrix is x = −a. So 4y² = 64x means y² = 16x, so a = 4.
**Ellipse (centre at origin).** **x²/a² + y²/b² = 1.** It is a stretched circle. If a > b, the long axis lies along x, and the foci are at (±c, 0) where c² = a² − b².

**Hyperbola (horizontal transverse axis).** **x²/a² − y²/b² = 1.** It has two separate branches. The foci are at (±c, 0) with **c² = a² + b²**. Notice the minus sign between the terms and the right side equal to +1. The form x²/a² − y²/b² = −1 opens up and down instead.

**The focus–directrix idea.** All three shapes can be described by an **eccentricity e**: a point moves so that its distance from the focus is e times its distance from the directrix. For a hyperbola e > 1, for an ellipse e < 1, for a parabola e = 1. For a hyperbola centred at the origin: **focus at (±ae, 0) and directrix at x = ±a/e.**

**Example.** Find the hyperbola with foci (±9, 0) and directrices x = ±4. Then ae = 9 and a/e = 4. Multiply: a² = 36. So a = 6 and e = 3/2. Then b² = c² − a² = 81 − 36 = 45. The equation is **x²/36 − y²/45 = 1.**
keyPoints: Parabola y² = 4ax. Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1.
Hyperbola: c² = a² + b², foci (±ae, 0), directrices x = ±a/e.
Ellipse: c² = a² − b².

example.problem: Find the foci of x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.
steps: It is an ellipse with a² = 25 and b² = 9.

sections.title: Tangent to a parabola
body: For the parabola **y² = 4ax**, the tangent at the point (x₁, y₁) **on the curve** is **y·y₁ = 2a(x + x₁).** This comes from replacing y² with y·y₁ and 2x with (x + x₁).

**Always check the point is on the curve first.** Take 4y² = 64x, which is y² = 16x with a = 4. The point (4, 8) is on it, because 8² = 64 = 16 × 4. The tangent there is 8y = 8(x + 4), so **y = x + 4.**

The point (3, 5) is **not** on y² = 16x, because 5² = 25 but 16 × 3 = 48. So a question asking for 'the tangent at (3, 5)' has a flaw, and you cannot find a tangent at a point that is not on the curve. If you meet a question like that, say the data is inconsistent, rather than forcing an answer.

A reliable check is that the tangent must **touch** the curve only once. Substitute y = x + 4 into y² = 16x: (x + 4)² = 16x gives x² − 8x + 16 = 0, which is (x − 4)² = 0, a single repeated root x = 4 ✓.
keyPoints: Tangent at (x₁, y₁) on y² = 4ax: yy₁ = 2a(x + x₁).
Check the point is on the curve first.

topics.intro: Kinematics describes how things move without asking why. You will use calculus to connect position, velocity and acceleration, work with motion in 2D and 3D by treating each direction separately, and use the standard formulae for constant acceleration.

sections.title: Motion in a straight line: position, velocity, acceleration
body: **Position** s tells you where an object is. **Velocity** v tells you how fast s changes, and **acceleration** a tells you how fast v changes. In calculus: **v = ds/dt** and **a = dv/dt = d²s/dt².** Going the other way, **integrate**: v = ∫a dt and s = ∫v dt.
**Differentiating** a power: d/dt (tⁿ) = n tⁿ⁻¹. So if s = 5t³ + 3t², then v = 15t² + 6t, and **a = 30t + 6.** At t = 3 s: a = 90 + 6 = **96 m/s².**

**Integrating** the other way: if v = 3t² + 4t, then s = t³ + 2t² + C. We know s = 0 at t = 0, so C = 0. At t = 5: s = 125 + 50 = **175 m.** The starting condition fixes the constant, and you must always use it.

**Turning points.** The object stops when v = 0. For s = t³ − 6t² + 9t, v = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), so it stops at t = 1 (s = 4) and t = 3 (s = 0). The acceleration a = 6t − 12 is −6 at t = 1, so the particle turns round there and moves backwards.
Units: if s is in metres and t in seconds, v is in **m/s** and a is in **m/s²**.
keyPoints: v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt; integrate to go backwards.
Use the starting condition to find the constant.
d/dt (tⁿ) = n tⁿ⁻¹.

sections.title: Motion in two and three dimensions
body: In 2D or 3D, the position is a **vector**: **r(t) = x(t)i + y(t)j + z(t)k.** Questions often write it as a column (x, y, z)ᵀ. To find velocity and acceleration, **differentiate each component separately.** To go back, integrate each component.

**Example (3D).** x = 3t², y = 8t, z = 2t³. Position at t = 2: **(12, 16, 16)** (x = 12, y = 16, z = 2 × 8 = 16). Velocity: v = (6t, 8, 6t²), which at t = 2 is (12, 8, 24). Acceleration: a = (6, 0, 12t), which at t = 2 is **(6, 0, 24).** Its magnitude is √(36 + 0 + 576) = **√612 m/s².**

**Example (2D).** x = 3t⁴ − 2t³ and y = 4t³ + 5t. Then v = (12t³ − 6t², 12t² + 5) and a = (36t² − 12t, 24t). At t = 4: v = (768 − 96, 192 + 5) = **(672, 197) m/s**, and a = (576 − 48, 96) = **(528, 96) m/s².** Keep both in order: x first, y second.

**Example (path with 3t²).** x = 3t² and y = 2t³ + 5t². At t = 2: position (12, 36); velocity (6t, 6t² + 10t) = **(12, 44)**; acceleration (6, 12t + 10) = **(6, 34).** Do not mix up the three: the position, velocity and acceleration use different formulas, and a question often asks for all three on the same curve.

**Exponential and trig motion.** x = e⁻ᵗ, y = 2cos 5t, z = 2 sin 5t. Derivatives: d/dt e⁻ᵗ = −e⁻ᵗ, d/dt 2cos 5t = −10 sin 5t, d/dt 2 sin 5t = 10 cos 5t. At t = 0: position (1, 2, 0), velocity (−1, 0, 10). Second derivatives: e⁻ᵗ, −50 cos 5t, −50 sin 5t, so acceleration at t = 0 is **(1, −50, 0).**

**Integrating a vector velocity.** A car has velocity (3t² + 5t, 2t + 3t³, t + 5t²) from the origin. Position = ∫v dt = (t³ + 5t²/2, t² + 3t⁴/4, t²/2 + 5t³/3). At t = 2: (8 + 10, 4 + 12, 2 + 40/3) = **(18, 16, 46/3) m.**
keyPoints: Differentiate each component for v and a; integrate each for position.
Check which one the question asks for: r, v or a.
Magnitude: √(sum of squares of components).

sections.title: Constant acceleration and the speed formulas
body: When acceleration is **constant**, there are four handy formulae (u = starting velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = distance): **v = u + at**, **s = ut + ½at²**, **v² = u² + 2as**, and **s = ½(u + v)t.**
**Example.** A car at 20 m/s accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. v = 20 + 12 = **32 m/s.** Distance: s = 20(4) + ½(3)(16) = 80 + 24 = **104 m.**
**Choosing the formula.** Write down what you know and what you want, and pick the formula that has exactly those letters. Each formula leaves out one of the five variables.
**Falling objects** have constant acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downwards. Take care with signs: choose a direction as positive (say upwards) and then a = −9.8.
These formulae are **only** for constant acceleration. When acceleration changes with time (like a = 30t + 6), you must use calculus instead.
keyPoints: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.
Only for constant acceleration.
Choose a positive direction and keep to it.

topics.intro: Force explains why things move. This lesson uses Newton's second law, F = ma, to find forces from motion, to find motion from a changing force, and to write the equations of motion for objects that fall or rise through air.

sections.title: Force, mass and acceleration
body: **Newton's second law:** the force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: **F = ma.** Force is measured in **newtons (N)** when mass is in kg and acceleration is in m/s². A force of 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Force is a vector, so for a particle moving in 2D or 3D we find the **acceleration vector** first, then multiply it by the mass: **F = m a.**

**Example.** A 20 kg particle follows x = 3t², y = 8t, z = 3t³. The acceleration is (6, 0, 18t) = (6, 0, 36) at t = 2. So **F = 20(6, 0, 36) = (120, 0, 720) N.** A common slip is to give the acceleration (6, 0, 36) as the force. Always multiply by the mass.
**Example.** A 10 kg particle with x = e⁻ᵗ, y = 2cos 5t, z = 2sin 5t. At t = 0 the acceleration is (1, −50, 0), so **F = (10, −500, 0) N.**

**Example.** A 4 kg particle with x = 3t⁴ − 2t³, y = 4t³ + 5t. At t = 4 the acceleration is (528, 96), so F = 4(528, 96) = **(2112, 384) N.** This is not among options like (528, 96) or (672, 197), which are acceleration and velocity.

**Which statements are true about force F?** (I) Force is the rate of change of momentum: **true**, F = d(mv)/dt. (II) Force is the same as impulse: **false**, impulse = force × time. (III) Force is mass × acceleration: **true.** (IV) Force is work done divided by displacement: **true**, because W = Fd along the motion. So the true ones are I, III and IV.
keyPoints: F = ma (and F = d(mv)/dt).
For motion in 2D/3D, find the acceleration vector, then multiply by the mass.
Impulse = force × time, not force.

sections.title: A force that changes with time
body: When the force depends on time, the acceleration does too. Use **a = F/m**, then integrate to get velocity, and again for distance. The particle's starting condition gives the constants.

**Example.** A 5 kg particle starts at rest. The force is (7t + t²) N. Then a = (7t + t²)/5. Integrate: **v = (7t²/2 + t³/3)/5 = 7t²/10 + t³/15**, since v = 0 when t = 0. Notice the division by 5 applies to every term.

**Impulse and momentum.** The impulse of a force is **force × time** (for a varying force, ∫F dt). It equals the **change in momentum**: ∫F dt = mv − mu. For the example above, ∫₀³ (7t + t²) dt = 31.5 + 9 = 40.5 N·s, and the momentum gained is 5 × 8.1 = 40.5 ✓.
If an option like 7t²/2 + t³/3 appears, it is the **impulse (momentum)**, not the velocity. You must still divide by the mass.
keyPoints: a = F/m, then integrate for v and again for s.
Use the starting conditions.
∫F dt is the impulse = change in momentum, and you must divide by m to get velocity.

sections.title: Writing equations of motion with air resistance
body: To write an **equation of motion**, draw the forces and apply **F = ma** in one chosen direction. Gravity pulls down with force **Mg**. Air resistance **opposes the motion**. The question may give it as Mkv (proportional to speed) or Mkv² (proportional to speed squared).
**Falling object** (take **downwards as positive**): gravity helps and air resistance opposes. M v′ = Mg − Mkv, so **v′ = g − kv.**

**Object shot upwards** (take **upwards as positive**): gravity pulls down (negative) and air resistance also acts downwards while the object rises. M v′ = −Mg − Mkv, so **v′ = −g − kv.** With resistance Mkv² the same logic gives **v′ = −g − kv².**

**The sign rule.** The sign depends on which direction you call positive. Gravity and resistance both point downwards on a rising object, so both terms are negative when up is positive. On a falling object they point in opposite directions, so there is a minus between them.
A quick check: as a falling object speeds up, v′ = g − kv shrinks to zero when v = g/k. That is the **terminal velocity**, a speed where the forces balance and the object stops accelerating.
keyPoints: Draw the forces, choose a positive direction, apply F = ma.
Upwards: v′ = −g − (resistance). Falling: v′ = g − (resistance).
Terminal velocity: set v′ = 0.

topics.intro: Work, energy and power link force and motion. You will calculate the work done by a force, kinetic energy, power in a moving particle, and work done against friction.

sections.title: Work, kinetic energy and power
body: **Work** is done when a force moves something. For a constant force along the direction of motion: **W = F × d.** The unit is the **joule (J)**: 1 joule is 1 newton moving 1 metre. If the force is at an angle θ to the motion, only the part along the motion counts: **W = F d cos θ** (this is the dot product F·d).

**Lifting work.** To lift a mass m through a height h, the force needed is its weight mg, so **W = mgh.** A 25 kg person climbing to a height of 3 m does W = 25 × 9.8 × 3 = **735 J.** Only the **vertical** height counts, so a staircase's horizontal distance (2 m here) is not used.
**Power** is the rate of doing work: **P = W/t**, measured in **watts (W)**. In the example, 735 J in 3 s gives P = 735/3 = **245 W.** Another formula: **P = F·v** (force times velocity).

**Kinetic energy** is the energy of motion: **KE = ½mv².** For a 10 kg particle with x = 5t and y = 3t, the velocity is (5, 3), so v² = 25 + 9 = 34 and KE = ½ × 10 × 34 = **170 J.** Use the **square of the magnitude** of the velocity, not the components separately.
**The work–energy theorem:** the net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy, **W = ΔKE.** If a 2 kg mass is speeding up from rest to 6 m/s, the work done is ½(2)(36) = 36 J.
keyPoints: W = Fd (W = Fd cos θ at an angle). Lifting: W = mgh.
P = W/t = F·v. KE = ½mv².
W = ΔKE.

sections.title: Power from force and velocity, and work against friction
body: For a particle whose force and velocity are vectors, **instantaneous power = F·v** (the dot product). Find F = ma, find v, then multiply matching components and add.

**Friction.** On a rough horizontal floor, the friction force is **μ × (normal force) = μmg**, where μ is the **coefficient of friction.** For an 80 kg load and μ = 0.4: friction = 0.4 × 80 × 9.8 = **313.6 N.** This is a **force** (in newtons), not work.

**Work done against friction** = friction force × **distance travelled along the path.** If the load moves from the origin to (9, 18), the distance is √(81 + 324) = 9√5 ≈ 20.1 m. Work against friction ≈ 313.6 × 20.1 ≈ **6,310 J.** Be careful to use the path distance, not just one coordinate.

**A warning.** In exam questions the quantities (mass, force, path) must agree with each other. If a question gives a force that does not match the motion (for example a force of (Z, 17) N acting on a 10 kg mass that moves with constant velocity, where the force must be zero), then the data is inconsistent and no honest answer exists.
keyPoints: Power = F·v for vectors.
Friction force = μmg; work against it = friction × path length.
The data in a question must be consistent.
